body:
What happens after IoT data is transmitted?

Collecting measurements is useful only when the information can support an appropriate purpose. An IoT platform is a software system that helps receive, organise, manage and use information from connected devices. Depending on the application, it may also manage authorised devices and send control commands.

A platform can support several functions:

  • Receiving readings and status messages from connected equipment.
  • Identifying the device associated with each reading.
  • Storing information for later comparison and analysis.
  • Displaying monitored conditions to authorised users.
  • Generating alerts when defined conditions are met.
  • Sending authorised control commands where the system permits them.

For example, a factory monitoring platform may receive motor-temperature readings from many machines. It can identify which machine reports an unusual condition and alert maintenance staff. The alert does not itself prove that the machine has failed; people or suitable systems must interpret it in context.

Cloud computing and edge processing

Cloud computing provides computing and storage resources through network-accessible services. An IoT platform may use cloud resources to store readings collected over long periods or to combine information from many locations.

Edge processing means processing data close to where it is generated, such as within a local controller or gateway. This can support faster local responses and reduce the need to send every raw measurement to a distant system.

FeatureEdge processingCloud processing
Usual locationNear the device or data sourceRemote computing infrastructure
Typical strengthLocal response with less network dependenceCentral storage and analysis across locations
ExampleLocal controller stops a pump when a condition is reachedPlatform compares irrigation records across fields

These approaches can work together. A local controller may respond immediately to a sensor condition, while selected records are also transmitted to a cloud platform for longer-term analysis. Cloud computing is not a compulsory component of every IoT system.

Interoperability: making different systems work together

Interoperability is the ability of different devices or systems to exchange information and use that information meaningfully. Successful transmission alone is not always enough. A receiving system must also understand what the information represents.

Suppose 2 soil-moisture devices from different manufacturers send readings to one platform. The platform needs to identify each device, interpret its readings correctly and apply an appropriate meaning to the reported values. If systems use incompatible formats or different interpretations, combining the data may be difficult.

Interoperability is especially important in smart cities and industries, where equipment from several suppliers may need to contribute information to a common platform.

Web of Things and artificial intelligence

The Web of Things (WoT) uses web technologies to make connected things and their services easier to access and integrate. It is related to IoT, but the terms are not identical: IoT is the wider concept of connected things, while WoT focuses on using web-based approaches for interaction and integration.

AI may be applied to IoT data to recognise patterns or support predictions, such as estimating when a machine might need maintenance. However, a platform that stores and displays sensor readings is not automatically using AI. A basic threshold alert can be generated through ordinary programmed rules.

Prelims focus

  • IoT platforms can manage data, devices, alerts and authorised control.
  • Cloud computing provides network-accessible computing and storage resources.
  • Edge processing takes place close to the data source.
  • Interoperability includes the ability to use exchanged information meaningfully.
  • WoT applies web technologies to connected things and their services.
  • Trap: Storing sensor data in the cloud does not, by itself, constitute AI.

[Sources: NCERT, Informatics Practices, Class 11, Chapter 2, sections 2.4.1 and 2.5, accessed 2026-11-05; ITU-T Recommendation Y.4218, May 2023, section 3.1, IoT definition and gateway functions, accessed 2026-11-05; ITU-T Recommendation Y.4122, Requirements of Edge Computing in IoT, July 2021, overview, accessed 2026-11-05.]

pictures.alt: A factory sensor feeds an edge controller for a possible local alert, while selected readings go to the cloud for history and staff review.
pictures.caption: Local decisions and central analysis can work together in one IoT system.

title: IoT Platforms, Cloud Computing, Edge Processing and Interoperability

body:
Smart agriculture

In agriculture, IoT can connect information about soil, weather, irrigation equipment and other field conditions. A soil-moisture monitoring device may help a farmer decide when irrigation is needed. Connected weather measurements can provide additional information for planning agricultural activities.

An automatic irrigation controller may use sensor information to operate a pump or valve under programmed conditions. The potential benefit is more informed use of water and equipment. Actual benefits depend on correct installation, suitable operating conditions and agricultural judgement.

Smart industry

Factories can connect machines and sensors so that operating information becomes available for maintenance and production planning. For instance, temperature or vibration readings from a motor can be monitored for changes that may indicate a developing problem.

Predictive maintenance uses information about equipment condition to help estimate when maintenance may be needed. It differs from routine maintenance performed at a fixed interval. Predictive systems do not guarantee that every fault will be detected in advance.

Industrial IoT is often called IIoT. It refers to IoT applications in industrial activities, not a completely different basic technology.

Connected healthcare

Healthcare applications can use connected devices to transmit measurements such as temperature, pulse or other relevant patient observations. A monitoring platform may display results to authorised healthcare workers and alert them when predefined conditions are detected.

Remote patient monitoring can support observation without requiring every reading to be taken during an in-person visit. However, the reliability of the device, accuracy of the measurement, protection of health information and professional interpretation remain essential. Connected monitoring does not replace clinical examination or diagnosis whenever those are necessary.

Smart homes and buildings

A connected building may use occupancy or environmental sensors to support lighting, ventilation, security monitoring or energy management. A connected smoke or environmental detector can send an alert to authorised users or a management system. These applications illustrate how IoT can be used for both information reporting and equipment control.

Smart cities: a genuine Gujarat example

A smart city uses information and communication technologies, including IoT where appropriate, to improve the planning, monitoring and management of public services. Possible applications include water supply, waste collection, transport, energy use, air-quality monitoring and public safety.

Surat, Gujarat, provides an example of integrated urban monitoring. Its Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC), also associated with the Surat Municipal Administrative Control (SMAC) Centre, brings information from different municipal services together for monitoring and coordinated action.

Surat's solid-waste-management system has used GPS-based vehicle tracking and radio-frequency identification (RFID) in related waste-management operations. GPS-based tracking supplies information about vehicle location and movement. RFID helps identify tagged objects or vehicles when they are read by suitable equipment. The resulting information can support monitoring, collection-route management and responses to missed services.

The distinction between the technologies matters. GPS provides positioning information, whereas RFID is primarily used for identification. Neither technology is synonymous with IoT by itself. They become useful parts of an integrated digital service when their information is communicated and used by the wider system.

In a smart city, sensors, identification technologies, communication networks, platforms and municipal staff may all have separate roles. A control centre does not mean that every city service operates autonomously.

Prelims focus

  • Industrial IoT applies connected monitoring and information systems to industrial activity.
  • Predictive maintenance uses equipment-condition information to help plan maintenance.
  • Remote patient monitoring transmits health-related measurements for appropriate review.
  • ICCC stands for Integrated Command and Control Centre.
  • Surat's municipal monitoring includes GPS-tracked waste-collection vehicles.
  • Trap: GPS provides location information; RFID primarily supports identification.

[Sources: NCERT, Informatics Practices, Class 11, Chapter 2, sections 2.4.2–2.4.3, accessed 2026-11-05; National Institute of Urban Affairs, Integrated Command and Control Centre, Surat Municipal Administrative Control Centre city profile, solid-waste-management and urban-governance sections, accessed 2026-11-05; NITI Aayog Frontier Tech, Cleaner Cities, Healthier Lives: How Surat's ICCC Is Advancing Urban Sanitation and Public Health, updated 16 July 2023, sections on RFID, GPS and waste-management monitoring, accessed 2026-11-05.]

title: Applications of IoT in Agriculture, Industry, Healthcare and Smart Cities

body:
Why government programmes matter

Digital technologies are applied in India through programmes involving urban services, electricity distribution, agriculture and the use of drones. For objective examinations, it is important to identify the responsible sector, the intended purpose and the difference between an approved target and work actually completed.

Smart Cities Mission and ICCCs

The Government of India launched the Smart Cities Mission on 25 June 2015. The mission sought to improve urban infrastructure and services through area-based development and suitable smart solutions. Technology is one part of such work; the mission is not exclusively an IoT programme.

Integrated Command and Control Centres (ICCCs) support coordinated monitoring and decision-making for city services, including mobility, water supply, sanitation, solid-waste management and public safety.

In a release dated 23 July 2026, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs reported that ICCCs had been operationalised across all 100 Smart Cities. This is the status reported on that date, rather than a separately established count for a later period.

In Gujarat, Surat's ICCC and its municipal monitoring systems provide a concrete example of the use of connected information for urban governance.

Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme and smart meters

The Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS) includes support for smart electricity metering. Unlike a conventional meter that requires someone to collect readings manually, a suitable connected smart meter can transmit consumption information for remote collection and processing.

Connected meter readings can support billing, electricity-distribution management and the identification of unusual consumption patterns. However, an individual reading must still be interpreted correctly; connectivity alone does not prove electricity theft or another fault.

The Ministry of Power reported the following Gujarat RDSS figures as of 15 July 2025 in a release published on 24 July 2025:

  • 1.67 crore smart meters sanctioned for Gujarat under RDSS.
  • 20.94 lakh smart meters installed as of the reported data date.

These figures describe different stages of implementation. Sanctioned means approved under the scheme; installed refers to units reported as installed. The July 2025 installation figure must not be presented as the current installation total for November 2026.

Digital Agriculture Mission

The Government of India approved the Digital Agriculture Mission on 2 September 2024 with an outlay of Rs 2,817 crore. Its purpose is to develop digital information and services that support agriculture.

Important components include AgriStack and the Krishi Decision Support System. AgriStack includes the Farmers' Registry, geo-referenced village maps and the Crop Sown Registry. The decision-support system is intended to bring together relevant information such as geospatial, weather and satellite data.

This mission is broader than IoT. Its digital records, mapping and decision-support functions are not all sensor-network applications. A digital database does not become an IoT device simply because it contains agricultural information.

Namo Drone Didi

Namo Drone Didi is a Central Sector Scheme intended to support women's self-help groups (SHGs) in providing agricultural drone services. The approved scheme has an outlay of Rs 1,261 crore for the period 2023-24 to 2025-26.

A Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare release dated 29 July 2025 described an overall approved target of 15,000 drones for women's SHGs. The proposed services include agricultural applications such as the spraying of suitable inputs by trained operators.

The figure of 15,000 describes the approved target, not a verified count of drones delivered. The scheme demonstrates an agricultural use of drone technology and a livelihood objective. It should not be classified as exclusively an IoT programme.

Government technology programmes must be classified by their actual purpose. Smart Cities Mission concerns urban development, RDSS concerns electricity distribution, Digital Agriculture Mission concerns agricultural digital infrastructure, and Namo Drone Didi concerns drone-based agricultural services and women's SHGs. These programmes may use emerging technologies without being identical to robotics or IoT.

Prelims focus

  • Smart Cities Mission was launched on 25 June 2015.
  • The government reported ICCCs operationalised across all 100 Smart Cities on 23 July 2026.
  • Gujarat RDSS figures as of 15 July 2025: 1.67 crore smart meters sanctioned and 20.94 lakh installed.
  • Digital Agriculture Mission was approved on 2 September 2024 with an outlay of Rs 2,817 crore.
  • Namo Drone Didi has an approved outlay of Rs 1,261 crore for 2023-24 to 2025-26 and an overall target of 15,000 drones.
  • Trap: Approved targets, sanctioned quantities and completed installations are not interchangeable.

[Sources: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, Press Information Bureau, Role of Integrated Command and Control Centres in Smart Cities, 23 July 2026, accessed 2026-11-05; Ministry of Power, Press Information Bureau, Smart Meters Installed Under RDSS, 24 July 2025, data as of 15 July 2025, accessed 2026-11-05; Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Press Information Bureau, Digital Agriculture Mission, 10 December 2024, approval and component details, accessed 2026-11-05; Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, Press Information Bureau, Implementation of Drone Didi Scheme, 29 July 2025, target and outlay, accessed 2026-11-05; Surat Municipal Corporation, Surat Smart City Mission overview, mission launch date, accessed 2026-11-05.]
